> 善為士者，不武；善戰者，不怒；善勝敵者，不與.

Four 不's in a row, and read as a list they sound like passive advice: don't fight, don't get angry, don't entangle, don't be proud.

The first one contains the oldest Chinese definition of warfare — and it was spoken by a man who had just won the largest battle of his life.

## 止戈為武

《左傳·宣公十二年》, the battle of 邲: the Chu army destroyed the Jin army.

Afterward, the minister 潘黨 proposed to King Zhuang of Chu: let us 築武軍 and 收晉尸以為京觀 — pile the Jin dead into a great mound so that our descendants will not forget this feat of arms.

The king refused. His reason is the line 說文 quotes:

夫文，止戈為武 — in the written character, 止 and 戈 make 武.

And 止 is the foot.

So 止戈為武 is not "to stop war." It is: the foot arrives at the spear and stops. You are holding the 戈, and the foot has halted.

## 不武 means the foot is stopped

Not "no weapon." The weapon is there. The chapter's claim is about the position of the foot: at the spear, and not past it.

Which is a very different kind of restraint from not being armed — and it is the only kind available to a king who has just won.

## 與 is a party of hands

與: 黨與也 — a faction, an alliance. And behind it the same image as 爭: 爭 is 引也, two hands pulling one object.

Contention needs a pair. A party needs a pair. Four hands on one thing.

Both require that there be an opponent.

## 不與 is not avoiding battle

It is: not giving the other side an opponent. Without an opponent, there is no contention — which is the same mechanism as chapter 66's 莫能與之爭.

## 善用人者，為之下

The fourth 不 is not a 不 at all: the one who uses people well puts himself below them.

The quartet is not four abstentions. It is: no display of force, no heat, no counterpart, and a lower position for the person you need.

## 士 is ten joined into one

士: 推十合一 — ten pushed into one.

The 士 is the one who can take ten things and bring them to a single conclusion — not a soldier, not a scholar, but the person whose function is consolidation.

Which makes 善為士者 a claim about a mind rather than a fighter: the one whose job is to unify is not the one who displays the spear.

## 是謂不爭之德，是謂用人之力，是謂配天

Not-contending 德; the strength of using others; being matched to heaven.

配 is to be paired with — the same pairing that 奇 (unpaired) denied. The one with no counterpart among men is paired with heaven.

古之極也 — the utmost of the ancients. 極 is the ridgepole, the highest beam.

## The chapter's actual subject

Read together, the four lines describe one thing: force that has no surface.

No display, no heat, no counterpart, no height. Each is a way of removing the thing that an opponent would use.

And the chapter is careful to note that this is not a technique for winning. It is a description of what remains when winning is not the point — which is why the last line is about heaven and not about victory.

## A test

Take one conflict you are in. Ask which of the four surfaces you are providing: a display, a heat, a pairing, a height. Removing one is usually enough to change the shape of it.
